meta.titre: Intermolecular Forces: London, Dipole and Hydrogen Bonding
meta.sous_theme: Types of force and their effect on boiling point

sections.contenu_markdown: Water in a cooking pot at a market stall in Douala boils at 100 degrees Celsius, although a water molecule is far smaller than a molecule of propane, the gas in a cooking-gas bottle, which boils at about 42 degrees below zero. Ethanol, sold as a disinfectant, boils at 78 degrees. These differences do not come from the covalent bonds inside the molecules, which stay intact, but from the weaker forces between molecules. Questions on intermolecular forces appear in almost every GCE Advanced Level paper, as a boiling point to explain, a solubility to justify or a trend to account for.

items: Electronegativity is the power of an atom to attract the bonding electrons; a bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar.
A molecule is polar overall only if its polar bonds do not cancel because of the shape of the molecule.
Melting and boiling involve changes of state, in which particles gain enough energy to move apart.
A lone pair is a pair of outer electrons not used in bonding.

sections.titre: Types of intermolecular force and how to compare them
sections.contenu_markdown:
Intermolecular forces are the attractions **between** molecules. They are much weaker than the covalent bonds **within** molecules: a typical covalent bond has an enthalpy of several hundred $\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, a hydrogen bond only about $20\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$. When a simple molecular substance melts or boils it is the intermolecular forces that are overcome; the covalent bonds stay intact. The stronger the forces, the more energy is needed and the higher the melting and boiling points.

**1. Instantaneous dipole-induced dipole forces (London or dispersion forces).** They act between all atoms and molecules. The electron cloud is constantly moving, so at any instant one side of a molecule is slightly more negative than the other (an instantaneous dipole). This induces a dipole in a neighbouring molecule and the two attract. The forces increase with the **number of electrons** (usually with the relative molecular mass), because a bigger electron cloud is more easily distorted, and with the **surface area** of contact, so straight chains attract more strongly than branched isomers.

**2. Permanent dipole-permanent dipole forces.** They act between polar molecules, such as HCl and propanone, where the $\delta+$ end of one molecule attracts the $\delta-$ end of another. Molecules with polar bonds that cancel by symmetry, for example $\mathrm{CO_2}$ and $\mathrm{CCl_4}$, are non-polar overall. Polar molecules also have London forces.

**3. Hydrogen bonding.** A hydrogen atom bonded to nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine is strongly $\delta+$ because these atoms are small and very electronegative. It is attracted to a lone pair on a nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine atom of a neighbouring molecule. The bond is written $\mathrm{X{-}H\cdots Y}$ (X and Y being N, O or F), and the three atoms lie close to a straight line. It is the strongest of the three intermolecular forces for molecules of similar size.

**Comparing substances.** First compare the electron count (or $M_r$); if similar, the substance with the extra, stronger type of force has the higher boiling point. For molecules of similar size the order of strength is: London forces only < permanent dipole forces < hydrogen bonding. In an answer, say which force exists **between the molecules**, say which is stronger, and state that **more energy is needed to overcome** it.

variantes.nom: Size and shape: how London forces vary
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a trend in boiling points is given for a homologous series, for halogens or noble gases, or for isomers with different shapes.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
| Alkane | Formula | Electrons | Boiling point / $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ (approx.) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Methane | $\mathrm{CH_4}$ | 10 | -162 |
| Ethane | $\mathrm{C_2H_6}$ | 18 | -89 |
| Propane | $\mathrm{C_3H_8}$ | 26 | -42 |
| Butane | $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$ | 34 | -1 |
| Pentane | $\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}$ | 42 | 36 |

As the chain lengthens the number of electrons increases, the instantaneous dipoles are larger, the London forces are stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules. The same reasoning explains why the halogens change from gases ($\mathrm{F_2}$, $\mathrm{Cl_2}$) to a liquid ($\mathrm{Br_2}$) and a solid ($\mathrm{I_2}$) down the group.

**Shape.** The isomers of $\mathrm{C_5H_{12}}$ have the same number of electrons, but pentane (36 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) boils higher than 2-methylbutane (about 28 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) and 2,2-dimethylpropane (about 10 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$). Branching makes the molecule more compact, reducing the surface area in contact with its neighbours, so the London forces are weaker.

variantes.nom: Hydrogen bonding in water, hydrogen fluoride, alcohols and acids
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a boiling point is unexpectedly high, when ice floats, or when a question asks you to draw or describe hydrogen bonds.
variantes.contenu_markdown:
**Water.** Each molecule has two hydrogen atoms bonded to oxygen and two lone pairs on oxygen, so it can form up to four hydrogen bonds. That is why water (boiling point 100 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) boils far above $\mathrm{H_2S}$ (about -60 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), although $\mathrm{H_2S}$ has more electrons. In ice each molecule is held by four hydrogen bonds in an open lattice with empty spaces, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats.

**Hydrogen fluoride.** HF boils at about 20 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, far above HCl (about -85 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$), HBr and HI, because of hydrogen bonding between HF molecules. For HCl, HBr and HI the boiling point rises with the number of electrons, as London forces strengthen.

**Alcohols and carboxylic acids.** Ethanol has an O-H group and boils at 78 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, much higher than ethanal (about 20 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) of almost the same $M_r$, which has no O-H bond. Carboxylic acids have both an O-H group and a C=O group, so two molecules can join in a hydrogen-bonded pair (a dimer); in a non-polar solvent such as benzene, ethanoic acid appears to have a relative molecular mass close to 120.

**Solubility.** Small alcohols and carboxylic acids dissolve in water because they form hydrogen bonds with water molecules. Hydrocarbons do not, because they cannot form hydrogen bonds and would only break the hydrogen bonds between water molecules.

variantes.nom: Hydrogen bonding is not shown by every molecule containing hydrogen
variantes.quand_utiliser: When deciding whether a given molecule can form hydrogen bonds with itself or with water.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Two conditions must both be met: a hydrogen atom bonded to N, O or F in the molecule, and a lone pair on N, O or F available in the neighbouring molecule. $\mathrm{CH_4}$ and $\mathrm{HCl}$ do not qualify because the hydrogen is bonded to carbon or chlorine. Methoxymethane, $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$, has oxygen with lone pairs but no O-H group, so its molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other (they do bond to water, which helps it dissolve). Its isomer ethanol has an O-H group and does hydrogen-bond, boiling at 78 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ against about -24 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ for the ether.

sections.enonce_markdown:
Butane, propanone and propan-1-ol have almost the same relative molecular mass. Their boiling points are -1 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, 56 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ and 97 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ respectively. ($A_r$: H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0.)

(a) Calculate the relative molecular mass and the number of electrons of each molecule.

(b) State the intermolecular forces present in each substance.

(c) Explain the order of the boiling points.

etapes.action: Calculate $M_r$ and the number of electrons.
etapes.justification: London forces depend on the number of electrons, so we need to know whether the three molecules are similar in size.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Butane $\mathrm{C_4H_{10}}$: $M_r = 58.0$, 34 electrons. Propanone $\mathrm{C_3H_6O}$: $M_r = 58.0$, 32 electrons. Propan-1-ol $\mathrm{C_3H_8O}$: $M_r = 60.0$, 34 electrons. The three have similar London forces.

etapes.action: Identify the forces in each substance.
etapes.justification: Check for polarity and for an H atom bonded to N, O or F.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Butane: non-polar, London forces only. Propanone: polar C=O group, permanent dipole-dipole forces as well as London forces; no O-H, so no hydrogen bonding. Propan-1-ol: London forces, permanent dipole forces and hydrogen bonds through its O-H group.

etapes.justification: With similar London forces, the extra force is responsible for the difference of $56 - (-1) = 57\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Propanone has permanent dipole-dipole attractions in addition to London forces, so more energy is needed to separate its molecules than those of butane.

etapes.justification: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than permanent dipole-dipole forces; the difference in boiling point is $97 - 56 = 41\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Between propan-1-ol molecules there are hydrogen bonds, $\mathrm{O{-}H\cdots O}$, so even more energy is needed to overcome the forces between molecules.

sections.conclusion_markdown: The boiling points increase in the order butane < propanone < propan-1-ol because the strongest intermolecular force changes from London forces to permanent dipole-dipole forces to hydrogen bonding, while the electron counts are almost the same. Only the forces between molecules are overcome; no covalent bond is broken.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that boiling water breaks the O-H covalent bonds, so water has a high boiling point.
items.pourquoi_faux: On boiling, the molecules stay intact. It is the hydrogen bonds between water molecules that are overcome; the covalent bonds are far too strong to be broken at 100 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.
items.correction_markdown: Water boils at 100 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ because a lot of energy is needed to overcome the hydrogen bonds between molecules.

items.erreur_markdown: Stating that $\mathrm{CH_4}$ and HCl form hydrogen bonds because they contain hydrogen.
items.pourquoi_faux: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O or F. In $\mathrm{CH_4}$ the C-H bond is almost non-polar; in HCl the chlorine atom is too large, with its charge spread over a big volume, to form a hydrogen bond.
items.correction_markdown: $\mathrm{CH_4}$ has London forces only; HCl has permanent dipole-dipole forces and London forces.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that HF has a lower boiling point than HI because HI has more electrons.
items.pourquoi_faux: The electron count only decides when the other forces are similar. HF is hydrogen-bonded, which outweighs the greater London forces in HI.
items.correction_markdown: HF (about 20 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) boils higher than HI (about -35 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) because of hydrogen bonding.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that London forces exist only in non-polar molecules.
items.pourquoi_faux: Every atom and molecule has electrons that move, so London forces act in all substances. Polar molecules have them in addition to dipole forces.
items.correction_markdown: London forces act between all molecules; they are the only force in non-polar substances such as butane and iodine.

items.erreur_markdown: Predicting that 2,2-dimethylpropane has a higher boiling point than pentane because its structure is more compact.
items.pourquoi_faux: A compact molecule has less surface area in contact with neighbouring molecules, so the instantaneous dipole attractions are weaker.
items.correction_markdown: Pentane (about 36 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) boils higher than 2,2-dimethylpropane (about 10 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$) because its straight chain allows greater contact.

items.enonce_markdown: State the strongest type of intermolecular force between molecules of each substance: (a) argon, (b) HCl, (c) $\mathrm{NH_3}$, (d) $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$, (e) $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) Argon atoms are non-polar: **London forces** only.

(b) HCl is polar: **permanent dipole-dipole forces** (and London forces).

(c) $\mathrm{NH_3}$ has N-H bonds and a lone pair on N: **hydrogen bonding**.

(d) $\mathrm{CH_3OCH_3}$ is polar, but there is no H bonded to O, N or F: **permanent dipole-dipole forces** (and London forces).

(e) $\mathrm{CH_3OH}$ has an O-H group: **hydrogen bonding**.

items.enonce_markdown:
The boiling points of the hydrides of group 16 are: $\mathrm{H_2O}$ 100 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $\mathrm{H_2S}$ -60 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $\mathrm{H_2Se}$ -41 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$, $\mathrm{H_2Te}$ -2 $^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$.

(a) Calculate the number of electrons in one molecule of each hydride.

(b) Explain the trend from $\mathrm{H_2S}$ to $\mathrm{H_2Te}$.

(c) Explain why the boiling point of water does not follow this trend.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $\mathrm{H_2O}$: 10; $\mathrm{H_2S}$: 18; $\mathrm{H_2Se}$: 36; $\mathrm{H_2Te}$: 54 electrons.

(b) From $\mathrm{H_2S}$ to $\mathrm{H_2Te}$ the number of electrons increases, so the instantaneous dipole-induced dipole (London) forces become stronger and more energy is needed to separate the molecules. The boiling point rises.

(c) Water molecules form hydrogen bonds, O-H$\cdots$O, because oxygen is small and highly electronegative and has lone pairs. Hydrogen bonds are much stronger than the forces in the other hydrides, so the boiling point of water is far higher than predicted from the number of electrons alone.

items.enonce_markdown:
(a) The relative molecular mass of ethanoic acid, $\mathrm{CH_3COOH}$, calculated from its formula is 60.0 ($A_r$: H = 1.0, C = 12.0, O = 16.0). When it is dissolved in benzene, a freezing point measurement gives an apparent value close to 120. Explain this, using a description of the bonding.

(b) Liquid water has a density of $1.00\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$ and ice has a density of $0.92\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}$. Calculate the volume of ice formed when $100\ \mathrm{g}$ of water freezes, and the percentage increase in volume. Explain why the volume increases.
items.solution_markdown:
(a) $M_r(\mathrm{CH_3COOH}) = 2(12.0) + 4(1.0) + 2(16.0) = 60.0$. In benzene, which cannot hydrogen-bond, two ethanoic acid molecules pair up: the O-H hydrogen atom of one molecule bonds to the C=O oxygen atom of the other, in two hydrogen bonds between the pair. The pair behaves as a single particle of relative mass $2 \times 60.0 =$ **120.0**, so the measured value is about 120.

(b) $100\ \mathrm{g}$ of liquid water occupies $\dfrac{100}{1.00} = 100\ \mathrm{cm^3}$. As ice, $V = \dfrac{100}{0.92} =$ **108.7 cm3**, an increase of $\dfrac{108.7 - 100}{100}\times100 =$ **8.7%**. In ice each molecule forms four hydrogen bonds in a fixed open, tetrahedral arrangement with empty space between the molecules; in liquid water the molecules are packed more closely.

items_markdown: Intermolecular forces act between molecules and are far weaker than covalent bonds; melting and boiling overcome the forces between molecules, not the bonds within them.

Three types: London (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) forces in all substances; permanent dipole-dipole forces in polar molecules; hydrogen bonding when H is bonded to N, O or F and a lone pair on N, O or F is available.
London forces increase with the number of electrons (size) and with surface contact: straight chains boil higher than branched isomers.
For molecules of similar size: London only < permanent dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding in strength and in boiling point.
Hydrogen bonding explains the high boiling points of water, HF, alcohols and acids, the low density of ice and the solubility of small alcohols in water.
